## 结论先行

两套文件体系都采用“动态试验（ATD）+ 可接受的分析方法”这一思路，但**适用范围、文件性质、排位差异和伤害准则的具体化程度不同**，不能合并成一条统一要求。Part 23 侧检索到的主要是 1980 年代至 1990 年代的规则制定讨论与一份 1989 年 AC；Part 25 侧检索到的是 2006 年 AC 及其 2015 年 Change 1，以及一份检查单。以下分别列明。

## 一、Part 23（小型飞机）

## 三、跨部分但不可合并的共性与差异

- **共同点**：AC 20-146A 对 14 CFR §§ 23.562、25.562、27.562、29.562 及 TSO-C127a/C127b 给出“经动态试验验证的计算机建模分析”这一**可接受但非唯一**的方法，并规定适用条件、限制、验证流程与最低文件要求 <kb doc="AC_20-146A.pdf" chunk_id="dcef9066-2587-4bee-a242-c3e355767659" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。该文件同时覆盖 Part 23 与 Part 25，但其本身是方法论 AC，不等于两部分的实体要求相同。
- **不可合并之处**：Part 23 以“第一排/其余排”区分严酷度 <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="ddecda8b-6472-489c-9662-c5da519a8bfc" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />；Part 25 检查单则按“前排除、排对排、出口排、乘务员、飞行机组”多类安装场景分别核查 <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。两者分类基础不同，不能互换。
- **未采用的材料**：23-45_DRS_90-18 讨论的是 23.365 增压舱与突然失压（会议提案 195），其中虽提到该提案“与 part 25 的类似现行要求平行”，但最终**撤回、不改 23.365(e)**，与座椅动态要求无直接关系 <kb doc="23-45_DRS_90-18.pdf" chunk_id="fc9aa567-6bca-4c6f-b982-babb5693c202" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-45_DRS_90-18.pdf" chunk_id="7b3c7783-00d5-4882-8a2e-9df4afca1cdf" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。

## 四、证据缺口（明确未知）

1. **Part 23 缺少数值准则**：检索到的 AC 23.562-1 仅有目的、相关法规与参考资料页 <kb doc="AC_23.562-1.pdf" chunk_id="9b1ed971-23e3-40f9-a290-9bf96bc47aa6" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />，未包含 HIC、股骨载荷、腰椎载荷等具体限值；23-36-DRS 也只讨论乘员质量与试验方式，未给出限值。因此无法说明 Part 23 的伤害准则数值是否与 Part 25 相同。
2. **Part 25 缺少适用范围定义原文**：检索片段未直接给出 Part 25 的运输类适用范围条款，也未给出 25.562 的限值原文；AC 25-17A 片段为检查单问题，属审查工具而非法规条文 <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。
3. **两份 AC 的现行有效性未证实**：AC 23.562-1 为 1989 年版，检索材料未显示其后续修订或被替代情况；AC 25.562-1B 的 Change 1 内容可见，但其完整正文与附录 2 变形限值未在检索片段中。
4. **23-36-DRS 的最终采纳状态未知**：文中反复使用“proposed”“when adopted”，检索材料未提供最终修正案号与生效日期，故上述 Part 23 要求应按“提案”而非“现行法规”引用。

**建议**：若需做合规性判定，应另行调取 14 CFR 23.562、25.562 的现行条文原文，以及 AC 23.562-1 的最新版本和 AC 25.562-1B 附录 2，方能补齐数值准则与适用范围的证据。

One commenter agreed in part with the proposal, stating that since the load in the pressure cabin is predictable, a reduction in the 150 percent safety factor might be justified. That commenter was opposed to total elimination of the 150 percent safety factor.
Another commenter objected to any reduction in the safety factor for ultimate loading below that already existing in part 23.
One commenter noted that conference proposal 194 was based on the pressure resulting from the maximum relief valve setting, which was usually higher than the operating pressure. That commenter felt that it was illogical to ask for 150 percent of that loading to be combined with the ultimate flight load since such a condition will never be achieved in real life.
Another commenter noted that, from a practical sense, the fatigue requirements generally design the cabin anyway. The proposed rule will not, in most cases, make any difference in design but will reduce the difficulty of testing to test to prove the design.

Another commenter pointed out that the limit cabin pressure without airloads is required to be 1.33 times the normal operating pressure. When increased to ultimate pressure using the 150 percent value, the fuselage pressure vessel must be designed for twice the maximum relief valve setting. This is true even with the two required pressure relief valves. That commenter noted that it was possible to obtain ultimate maneuver load on the airframe but contended that there was no practical way to get ultimate pressure in the pressure vessel. That commenter was unaware of any airplane that had the capability of pressurizing the pressure vessel to twice the relief valve setting. That commenter was of the opinion that conference proposal 194 had merit.
The FAA has reviewed conference proposal 194 and the philosophical intent of the 150 percent safety factor used for ultimate load testing. The FAA finds that the 150 percent increase must be applied to design service conditions to provide a factor of safety beyond the limit condition. The probability of whether or not the 150 percent load is operationally obtainable is not related to the intent of this safety factor. The design condition of full maneuver loads on a pressurized cabin constitutes the design service condition and, as such, the 150 percent safety factor is appropriate. Accordingly, no change is proposed to Section 23.365(a).

Conference proposal 195 recommends revising Section 23.365(e) to (1) reword existing paragraph (e); (2) include consideration of cabin penetration due to the probability of engine disintegration, and (3) require consideration of the probability of detachment of parts of the airplane resulting in passenger injury during sudden decompression. This proposal parallels particular similar existing part 25 requirements.
Items (2) and (3) were strongly opposed by commenters at the conference primarily because of the small cabin volume of part 23 airplanes when compared to the volume of part 25 airplanes. One commenter stated that decompression tests run on part 25 business jets (cabin volumes similar to part 23 airplanes) indicated very little movement of the anthropomorphic dummies or the cabin contents. That commenter stated that, in some cases, the sleeve on the anthropomorphic dummy was noted to move and, in one case, a piece of paper shifted aft a couple of inches.

Another commenter contended that there was no practical design that would prevent penetration of the cabin when a complete engine deterioration occurred.
Post conference review indicates that, in practical small airplane designs, the effects of cabin
depressurization are sufficiently difference from those of transport category airplanes to justify differences in the requirements. However, Report AM 67-14 entitled "An Evaluation of Potential Decompression Hazards in Small Pressurized Aircraft", published by the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of Aviation Medicine, June 1967, indicates that during sudden decompression, the volumes of even small pressurized aircraft are sufficient to cause passenger ejections from the aircraft, fatal injuries from head impact, concussion and unconsciousness, and, in some cases, even lung rupture. The report recommends considering double-pane windows and plug type exits on all pressurized airplanes. Specific requirements for windows in pressurized airplanes were added by amendment 23-7, effective 1969 and changes to door locking mechanisms have been adopted into part 23 by amendment No. 1 of the Small Airplane Airworthiness Program, (amendment 23-36, 53 FR 30802; august 15, 1988). Therefore, no change is proposed to existing Section 23.365(e) and conference proposal 195 is withdrawn.

Reference: Conference proposals 194 and 195.
No action is being taken to amend Section 23.373 Speed control devices.
Explanation: Conference proposal 196 proposes to revise Section 23.373(a) for all small airplanes having gross weights in excess of 6,000 pounds to increase the deployment speed of speed control devices from the currently allowed placard speed chosen during certification to the design dive speed V_D
In support of conference proposal 196, the submitter notes that designs have been previously approved that have placarded speeds no higher than V_C . The submitter doubts that anyone deliberately flies at V_D. but contends that existing requirements demand load investigations to V_D because high speed upsets do occur for whatever reason, and aircraft do exceed the maximum airspeed operating limits. The submitter argues that, in such cases, the pilot may use any speed control device available to avoid an excessive overspeed situation in spite of being at the maximum placarded speed. One commenter noted that the condition described by the submitter is not a normal incident and that existing safety factors allow some margin for error.

One commenter agreed in part with the proposal, stating that since the load in the pressure cabin is predictable, a reduction in the 150 percent safety factor might be justified. That commenter was opposed to total elimination of the 150 percent safety factor.
Another commenter objected to any reduction in the safety factor for ultimate loading below that already existing in part 23.
One commenter noted that conference proposal 194 was based on the pressure resulting from the maximum relief valve setting, which was usually higher than the operating pressure. That commenter felt that it was illogical to ask for 150 percent of that loading to be combined with the ultimate flight load since such a condition will never be achieved in real life.
Another commenter noted that, from a practical sense, the fatigue requirements generally design the cabin anyway. The proposed rule will not, in most cases, make any difference in design but will reduce the difficulty of testing to test to prove the design.

Another commenter pointed out that the limit cabin pressure without airloads is required to be 1.33 times the normal operating pressure. When increased to ultimate pressure using the 150 percent value, the fuselage pressure vessel must be designed for twice the maximum relief valve setting. This is true even with the two required pressure relief valves. That commenter noted that it was possible to obtain ultimate maneuver load on the airframe but contended that there was no practical way to get ultimate pressure in the pressure vessel. That commenter was unaware of any airplane that had the capability of pressurizing the pressure vessel to twice the relief valve setting. That commenter was of the opinion that conference proposal 194 had merit.
The FAA has reviewed conference proposal 194 and the philosophical intent of the 150 percent safety factor used for ultimate load testing. The FAA finds that the 150 percent increase must be applied to design service conditions to provide a factor of safety beyond the limit condition. The probability of whether or not the 150 percent load is operationally obtainable is not related to the intent of this safety factor. The design condition of full maneuver loads on a pressurized cabin constitutes the design service condition and, as such, the 150 percent safety factor is appropriate. Accordingly, no change is proposed to Section 23.365(a).

Conference proposal 195 recommends revising Section 23.365(e) to (1) reword existing paragraph (e); (2) include consideration of cabin penetration due to the probability of engine disintegration, and (3) require consideration of the probability of detachment of parts of the airplane resulting in passenger injury during sudden decompression. This proposal parallels particular similar existing part 25 requirements.
Items (2) and (3) were strongly opposed by commenters at the conference primarily because of the small cabin volume of part 23 airplanes when compared to the volume of part 25 airplanes. One commenter stated that decompression tests run on part 25 business jets (cabin volumes similar to part 23 airplanes) indicated very little movement of the anthropomorphic dummies or the cabin contents. That commenter stated that, in some cases, the sleeve on the anthropomorphic dummy was noted to move and, in one case, a piece of paper shifted aft a couple of inches.

Another commenter contended that there was no practical design that would prevent penetration of the cabin when a complete engine deterioration occurred.
Post conference review indicates that, in practical small airplane designs, the effects of cabin
depressurization are sufficiently difference from those of transport category airplanes to justify differences in the requirements. However, Report AM 67-14 entitled "An Evaluation of Potential Decompression Hazards in Small Pressurized Aircraft", published by the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of Aviation Medicine, June 1967, indicates that during sudden decompression, the volumes of even small pressurized aircraft are sufficient to cause passenger ejections from the aircraft, fatal injuries from head impact, concussion and unconsciousness, and, in some cases, even lung rupture. The report recommends considering double-pane windows and plug type exits on all pressurized airplanes. Specific requirements for windows in pressurized airplanes were added by amendment 23-7, effective 1969 and changes to door locking mechanisms have been adopted into part 23 by amendment No. 1 of the Small Airplane Airworthiness Program, (amendment 23-36, 53 FR 30802; august 15, 1988). Therefore, no change is proposed to existing Section 23.365(e) and conference proposal 195 is withdrawn.

Reference: Conference proposals 194 and 195.
No action is being taken to amend Section 23.373 Speed control devices.
Explanation: Conference proposal 196 proposes to revise Section 23.373(a) for all small airplanes having gross weights in excess of 6,000 pounds to increase the deployment speed of speed control devices from the currently allowed placard speed chosen during certification to the design dive speed V_D
In support of conference proposal 196, the submitter notes that designs have been previously approved that have placarded speeds no higher than V_C . The submitter doubts that anyone deliberately flies at V_D. but contends that existing requirements demand load investigations to V_D because high speed upsets do occur for whatever reason, and aircraft do exceed the maximum airspeed operating limits. The submitter argues that, in such cases, the pilot may use any speed control device available to avoid an excessive overspeed situation in spite of being at the maximum placarded speed. One commenter noted that the condition described by the submitter is not a normal incident and that existing safety factors allow some margin for error.

B. Aviation Rulemaking Committee
(ARC) Recommendations On February 3, 2003, we published a notice announcing the creation of the part 125/135 Aviation Rulemaking

Committee.1 Part 125 addresses the certification and operations of airplanes having a seating capacity of 20 or more passengers or a maximum payload capacity of 6,000 pounds or more. Part 135 addresses the operating requirements for commuter and on-demand operations and rules governing persons on board such aircraft. That commenter felt that it was illogical to ask for 150 percent of that loading to be combined with the ultimate flight load since such a condition will never be achieved in real life.
Another commenter noted that, from a practical sense, the fatigue requirements generally design the cabin anyway. The proposed rule will not, in most cases, make any difference in design but will reduce the difficulty of testing to test to prove the design.

Another commenter pointed out that the limit cabin pressure without airloads is required to be 1.33 times the normal operating pressure. When increased to ultimate pressure using the 150 percent value, the fuselage pressure vessel must be designed for twice the maximum relief valve setting. This is true even with the two required pressure relief valves. That commenter noted that it was possible to obtain ultimate maneuver load on the airframe but contended that there was no practical way to get ultimate pressure in the pressure vessel. That commenter was unaware of any airplane that had the capability of pressurizing the pressure vessel to twice the relief valve setting. That commenter was of the opinion that conference proposal 194 had merit.
The FAA has reviewed conference proposal 194 and the philosophical intent of the 150 percent safety factor used for ultimate load testing. The FAA finds that the 150 percent increase must be applied to design service conditions to provide a factor of safety beyond the limit condition. The probability of whether or not the 150 percent load is operationally obtainable is not related to the intent of this safety factor. The design condition of full maneuver loads on a pressurized cabin constitutes the design service condition and, as such, the 150 percent safety factor is appropriate. Accordingly, no change is proposed to Section 23.365(a).

Conference proposal 195 recommends revising Section 23.365(e) to (1) reword existing paragraph (e); (2) include consideration of cabin penetration due to the probability of engine disintegration, and (3) require consideration of the probability of detachment of parts of the airplane resulting in passenger injury during sudden decompression. This proposal parallels particular similar existing part 25 requirements.
Items (2) and (3) were strongly opposed by commenters at the conference primarily because of the small cabin volume of part 23 airplanes when compared to the volume of part 25 airplanes. One commenter stated that decompression tests run on part 25 business jets (cabin volumes similar to part 23 airplanes) indicated very little movement of the anthropomorphic dummies or the cabin contents. That commenter stated that, in some cases, the sleeve on the anthropomorphic dummy was noted to move and, in one case, a piece of paper shifted aft a couple of inches.

Another commenter contended that there was no practical design that would prevent penetration of the cabin when a complete engine deterioration occurred.
Post conference review indicates that, in practical small airplane designs, the effects of cabin
depressurization are sufficiently difference from those of transport category airplanes to justify differences in the requirements. However, Report AM 67-14 entitled "An Evaluation of Potential Decompression Hazards in Small Pressurized Aircraft", published by the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of Aviation Medicine, June 1967, indicates that during sudden decompression, the volumes of even small pressurized aircraft are sufficient to cause passenger ejections from the aircraft, fatal injuries from head impact, concussion and unconsciousness, and, in some cases, even lung rupture. The report recommends considering double-pane windows and plug type exits on all pressurized airplanes. Specific requirements for windows in pressurized airplanes were added by amendment 23-7, effective 1969 and changes to door locking mechanisms have been adopted into part 23 by amendment No. 1 of the Small Airplane Airworthiness Program, (amendment 23-36, 53 FR 30802; august 15, 1988). Therefore, no change is proposed to existing Section 23.365(e) and conference proposal 195 is withdrawn.

Reference: Conference proposals 194 and 195.
No action is being taken to amend Section 23.373 Speed control devices.
Explanation: Conference proposal 196 proposes to revise Section 23.373(a) for all small airplanes having gross weights in excess of 6,000 pounds to increase the deployment speed of speed control devices from the currently allowed placard speed chosen during certification to the design dive speed V_D
In support of conference proposal 196, the submitter notes that designs have been previously approved that have placarded speeds no higher than V_C . The submitter doubts that anyone deliberately flies at V_D. but contends that existing requirements demand load investigations to V_D because high speed upsets do occur for whatever reason, and aircraft do exceed the maximum airspeed operating limits. The submitter argues that, in such cases, the pilot may use any speed control device available to avoid an excessive overspeed situation in spite of being at the maximum placarded speed. One commenter noted that the condition described by the submitter is not a normal incident and that existing safety factors allow some margin for error.

## 结论先行

两套文件体系都采用“动态试验（ATD）+ 可接受的分析方法”这一思路，但**适用范围、文件性质、排位差异和伤害准则的具体化程度不同**，不能合并成一条统一要求。Part 23 侧检索到的主要是 1980 年代至 1990 年代的规则制定讨论与一份 1989 年 AC；Part 25 侧检索到的是 2006 年 AC 及其 2015 年 Change 1，以及一份检查单。以下分别列明。

## 一、Part 23（小型飞机）

| 维度 | 内容 | 来源/证据状态 |
|---|---|---|
| 适用范围与文件性质 | AC 23.562-1《DYNAMIC TESTING OF PART 23 AIRPLANE SEAT/RESTRAINT SYSTEMS AND OCCUPANT PROTECTION》，1989-06-22，涉及 23.562、23.785、23.787；明确为“可接受但非唯一”的符合性信息与指导，**非强制、非法规** | <kb doc="AC_23.562-1.pdf" chunk_id="9b1ed971-23e3-40f9-a290-9bf96bc47aa6" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 乘员质量 | 动态试验采用 170 lb（第 50 百分位男性）；215 lb 仅用于座椅**静载**试验，以验证正常飞行与地面使用中的功能 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="524f45a1-f00b-4f93-b714-61870988d54c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="74f7cc02-7f24-43b3-b55d-032e78ec174b" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 排位差异 | 第一排座椅的动态载荷试验要求比其余排更严；理由是越靠后，碰撞载荷一般越小，机翼梁常是结构压溃停止点 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="ddecda8b-6472-489c-9662-c5da519a8bfc" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 朝向与特殊布置 | 后向、侧向座椅若能满足全部要求应获批准；非前向座椅试验时，座椅相对冲击矢量的对齐应与机上预期朝向一致 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="59ea662b-78fb-4e62-b718-d302fb56e81c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="11177de5-0e01-46e8-a96a-b1b9e58cb59b" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 卧铺（litter） | 因 40 CFR Part 572 的 ATD 为坐姿、髋部不可旋转，无法模拟卧姿，动态试验不可行；改为在拟议 23.785 中提高卧铺连接件的极限静载系数 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="59ea662b-78fb-4e62-b718-d302fb56e81c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="541137d7-c524-4104-a8b1-5709d587b19d" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 分析替代试验 | 拟议 23.562(d) 旨在为“分析技术成熟后替代动态试验”提供灵活性，允许基于既往已批准动态试验设计的合理分析；但当时与会意见及 FAA 均认为数据库不足，仍需动态试验 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="59ea662b-78fb-4e62-b718-d302fb56e81c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="11177de5-0e01-46e8-a96a-b1b9e58cb59b" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 生效与追溯 | 新要求自修正案生效日起适用，**不追溯**至 GASP 建议的 1985-12-31 | <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="524f45a1-f00b-4f93-b714-61870988d54c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="60cb118e-3596-40d8-8509-b51419b7980e" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |

**性质提示**：上述 23.562(d)、23.785 等内容出自规则制定讨论文件（23-36-DRS_86-19），文中使用“proposed Section”“when adopted”等措辞，属于**提案阶段的讨论与 FAA 结论**，不等同于已生效的法规条文。

## 二、Part 25（运输类飞机）

| 维度 | 内容 | 来源/证据状态 |
|---|---|---|
| 适用范围与文件性质 | AC 25.562-1B《Dynamic Evaluation of Seat Restraint Systems and Occupant Protection on Transport Airplanes》，2006-01-10（Change 1，2015-09-30），提供 14 CFR part 25 座椅动态试验的可接受符合性方法，并说明试验程序背后的理由、所需试验设施与设备 | <kb doc="AC_25.562-1B.pdf" chunk_id="11a60e78-5f63-4d8e-8b47-33981454f982" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 审查项（25.562） | 检查单逐项核查：座椅是否有 TSO-C127/C127a 批准及正确座位类型标记、坐垫与约束系统件号、前向/后向；安装限制是否覆盖前排除、排对排、出口排、乘务员、飞行机组等；机上座椅导轨件号是否与动态试验所用一致，否则需等效或更优的证实数据；永久变形是否超出 AC 25.562-1B 附录 2 限值并影响排距、出口排、最小通道宽度等；每个座位（乘客、乘务员、飞行机组）的伤害准则是否满足 | <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 伤害准则 | 检查单明确列出 HIC、股骨、腰椎、安全带载荷 | <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| HIC 符合性方法 | Change 1 删除了 5e(5)(d) 中“错误发放”的方法，因其可能使全部所需乘员范围得不到同等头部保护，且与政策备忘录 ANM-115-05-14（前排除 HIC）冲突；排对排仍可用附录 4 简化方法；新增前排除 42"/45" 间距准则适用说明 | <kb doc="AC_25.562-1B.pdf" chunk_id="88c0ca08-c58e-4bde-bffa-1222b69857cf" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 其他新增指导 | 明确应处理的偏航角范围；对乘员范围须使用“solid strike”证明符合性；在 5e(5)(a) 及附录 4 增加上部躯干约束与气囊指导 | <kb doc="AC_25.562-1B.pdf" chunk_id="9d95cfa4-aaeb-45f0-a6ad-01f2fca7af8d" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |
| 25.785 相关 | 检查单另列：头部可及范围内潜在致伤物、扶手、脚凳/腿凳/头枕、安全带、乘务员肩带、直接视野、扶手把手、突出物包覆、乘务员座椅靠近地板高度出口等 | <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="10f3a630-82d9-481d-bb13-64742282d93c" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /> |

## 三、跨部分但不可合并的共性与差异

- **共同点**：AC 20-146A 对 14 CFR §§ 23.562、25.562、27.562、29.562 及 TSO-C127a/C127b 给出“经动态试验验证的计算机建模分析”这一**可接受但非唯一**的方法，并规定适用条件、限制、验证流程与最低文件要求 <kb doc="AC_20-146A.pdf" chunk_id="dcef9066-2587-4bee-a242-c3e355767659" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。该文件同时覆盖 Part 23 与 Part 25，但其本身是方法论 AC，不等于两部分的实体要求相同。
- **不可合并之处**：Part 23 以“第一排/其余排”区分严酷度 <kb doc="23-36-DRS_86-19.pdf" chunk_id="ddecda8b-6472-489c-9662-c5da519a8bfc" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />；Part 25 检查单则按“前排除、排对排、出口排、乘务员、飞行机组”多类安装场景分别核查 <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。两者分类基础不同，不能互换。
- **未采用的材料**：23-45_DRS_90-18 讨论的是 23.365 增压舱与突然失压（会议提案 195），其中虽提到该提案“与 part 25 的类似现行要求平行”，但最终**撤回、不改 23.365(e)**，与座椅动态要求无直接关系 <kb doc="23-45_DRS_90-18.pdf" chunk_id="fc9aa567-6bca-4c6f-b982-babb5693c202" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" /><kb doc="23-45_DRS_90-18.pdf" chunk_id="7b3c7783-00d5-4882-8a2e-9df4afca1cdf" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。

## 四、证据缺口（明确未知）

1. **Part 23 缺少数值准则**：检索到的 AC 23.562-1 仅有目的、相关法规与参考资料页 <kb doc="AC_23.562-1.pdf" chunk_id="9b1ed971-23e3-40f9-a290-9bf96bc47aa6" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />，未包含 HIC、股骨载荷、腰椎载荷等具体限值；23-36-DRS 也只讨论乘员质量与试验方式，未给出限值。因此无法说明 Part 23 的伤害准则数值是否与 Part 25 相同。
2. **Part 25 缺少适用范围定义原文**：检索片段未直接给出 Part 25 的运输类适用范围条款，也未给出 25.562 的限值原文；AC 25-17A 片段为检查单问题，属审查工具而非法规条文 <kb doc="AC_25-17A_part04_p0601-0800.pdf" chunk_id="a1117869-380e-4859-8115-07984e10ee26" kb_id="acdf013d-971b-42c3-b6ca-cf09157c9215" />。
3. **两份 AC 的现行有效性未证实**：AC 23.562-1 为 1989 年版，检索材料未显示其后续修订或被替代情况；AC 25.562-1B 的 Change 1 内容可见，但其完整正文与附录 2 变形限值未在检索片段中。
4. **23-36-DRS 的最终采纳状态未知**：文中反复使用“proposed”“when adopted”，检索材料未提供最终修正案号与生效日期，故上述 Part 23 要求应按“提案”而非“现行法规”引用。

**建议**：若需做合规性判定，应另行调取 14 CFR 23.562、25.562 的现行条文原文，以及 AC 23.562-1 的最新版本和 AC 25.562-1B 附录 2，方能补齐数值准则与适用范围的证据。
